We need to get to 225 from 24. So where do we start? Well, easy enough, get to a round number to start out with by adding 6. We're at 30. Add 70, we're up to 100. Add another 100, we're at 200. Lastly, add 25. We're at 225. Now we take all those numbers we've used (6, 70, 100, and 25), and add them together, and we get our solution. 201.

That method really shines when you have carryover, for example, 225 - 29. In the math we learned as kids, it would end out being something like-

225 - 29 to 21(15) - 29 which establishes the number in the ones spot as 6. Then we get 216 - 20 = 196.

which can definitely be confusing to learn initially, and can get much more irritating if that happens with multiple parts in the problem.

In the number line example, it changes to getting to 225 from 29. Add 6. We're at 35. Add 100. We're at 135. Add 90. We're at 225. 6+100+90 = 196. Easy.

Frankly I'm all for learning new ways to do shit, since they can be effective in different situations (as I just showed.). Learning other ways (like the number line.) helps with learning how to manipulate equations so that down the line they don't develop an unhealthy relationship with X and Y.

Also, the method we've all grown up with is considered the standard algorithm, and kids are expected to have mastered it by 4th grade.

First of all, I think common core is crap.

That said I understand what they're trying to teach is how someone would do this in their head. Unfortunately, a) that only works for problems you can do in your head and b) they teach the method as if there is only one "right" way to do it in your head which just makes it even more confusing.

For instance, given the problem in the link, most (pre-common core) people won't line it up in there head and to columnwise subtraction. Most people (I believe) would break it into two parts and think to themselves

(25-24) = 1

1 + 200 = 201

It is this process of breaking the problem up that common core is trying to teach. But as I said previously, where they fail is they teach that there is only one way to do it. For the linked problem common core is basically asking in a convoluted manner:

225 - 24 = x

24 + x = 225

Then solve for 'x' in nice simple steps (usually multiples of 10, not that they actually explain what a multiple of 10 is to kids....).

so we want to make 24 a multiple of 10. That means adding 6 to get 30

24+6 = 30

now we want to get to 100, so add 70

24 + 6 + 70 = 100

then 200,

24 + 6 + 70 + 100 = 200

then add the 25

24 + 6 +70 +100 + 25 = 225

which brings us back to 24 + x = 225

24 + (6 + 70 + 100 +25 ) = 225

x = (6 + 70 + 100 + 25 )

225 - 24 = x = 201

Now the linked example is a bit disingenuous because there is no borrowing such that anyone with 2 brain cells can do it the "normal" way without thinking.

Now if it was say 225 - 28 it gets mildly more complicated.

Doing it the traditional mechanical way requires "borrowing" which is a simple enough operation to work through on paper (and one I still believe they should teach) but it does become cumbersome to do in your head.

Myself, I would still just break it into 2 parts in my head.

25 - 28 = -3

200 - 3 = 197

However, many people have problems with negative numbers, so this could be confusing for some.

The common core method does give a mechanical, although needlessly busy, way of doing it:

Again we're basically solving 225 - 28 = x, or

28 + x = 225

so get to a multiple of 10.

28 + 2 = 30

28 + 2 + 70 = 100

28 + 2 + 70 + 100 = 200

28 + 2 + 70 + 100 + 25 = 225

x = 2 + 70 + 100 + 25

x = 197

That said, all you're really doing is converting a simple enough subtraction into (what the formers of common core believe is) a slightly less complicated addition problem. At least that's the theory.
